Signature Cure Study Ballot Rejection Project · 2014–2024

Ballot Rejection Project

Thirty states now let a voter fix a mail ballot whose signature didn't match, instead of throwing it out. Using six years of official election data, this project looked for the drop in rejection rates that should follow — checking the answer three separate ways. All three say the drop isn't there.

The question

A mail ballot can fail for many reasons: it arrives late, it's missing a witness signature, or — the case that generates the most litigation — the signature on the envelope doesn't look enough like the one on file.

A signature-cure law is the obvious fix. Which would notify the voter and give them a window, usually three to seven days after the election, to confirm their identity and have the ballot counted. It's cheap, uncontroversial in principle, and has spread to a majority of states.

So have signature-cure law decrease mail ballot rejection rates? This project matched a state-by-jurisdiction panel of rejection rates against the year each state's cure requirement took effect and determined that many states have seen limited differences in rejection rates.

Three ways of checking the answer

Getting the same answer from one statistical method isn't very convincing on its own — a method can have a blind spot that happens to point the wrong way. So this project checked the answer three different ways, each one built to catch a different kind of mistake the others could make.

Method 01

Two-way fixed effects

The standard comparison: each state and each election year is compared against its own average, so only the leftover change matters.

Its blind spot: when states adopt a law in different years (as here), this method can accidentally treat states that already have the law as a "before" comparison for states that just got it — which quietly pulls the estimate toward zero even if a real effect exists. This is the baseline method, included so the other two can be checked against it, not the one to trust most.

Method 02

Sun & Abraham (2021)

A newer method built specifically to fix Method 01's blind spot: it measures each state's effect separately based on how many years it's had the law, then averages those together properly. Excludes Iowa (which adopted, then repealed the law) and the 13 states that already had it before this data begins.

Its blind spot: the average can still be skewed if a few states with unusual results happen to carry more weight than the rest.

Method 03

Callaway & Sant'Anna (2021)

The most cautious method: it only ever compares a state to others that haven't adopted the law yet (or never will), never to a state that already has it — the cleanest possible comparison.

Its blind spot: being this careful means throwing away some comparisons, so its results are naturally a bit less precise than the other two.

Figure 5

Where rejections actually happen

Most elections in most places reject well under 2% of mail ballots. There simply isn't much rejection left to eliminate — and what little there is varies much more from place to place than it does from year to year in the same place.

Ruling out rural/urban divide

An earlier check split states into "large" and "small" jurisdictions as a rough stand-in for urban and rural, but that split turned out to be unreliable — the smallest jurisdictions were missing entire groups of states, making the comparison meaningless. This round redoes the same check using each county's real government classification of urban vs. rural, with every group of states properly represented.

Why this "no effect" finding holds up

A common worry with a study like this is that it just wasn't sensitive enough to catch a real effect. That's not the case here: with this much data, an effect anywhere close to what cure-law supporters expected would have shown up clearly in all three methods. It didn't.

The rural-vs-urban check above is also worth reading carefully rather than at face value. An earlier version of that check was unreliable for a purely mechanical reason (some groups of states were missing from the comparison). Fixing that problem didn't turn up a hidden effect either — it's still no in both rural and urban areas. That should be read as "this doesn't detect a difference by rurality," not as final proof no difference could ever exist anywhere.

So the honest, careful version of this finding is narrower than the headline suggests: signature-cure laws, as states have actually written and run them, have not measurably changed how many mail ballots get rejected. That leaves open a related but different question this data can't answer: whether curing works well for the specific voters who actually get notified. Answering that would need records most states don't currently publish — how many voters were notified, and how many of them successfully fixed their ballot.

What would change this conclusion

Records of how many voters were actually notified under a cure law, and how many of them successfully fixed their ballot. If most notified voters never respond, that would point to a real problem the state-level numbers can't see.

Income, age, and education data for each county (already collected for this project) used to adjust the estimates directly, not just to split states into groups.

More years of data. Some states have only had the law in place for a couple of elections so far, which limits how much can be said about its long-run effect.

Clearer information on the handful of states (Illinois, Massachusetts, Ohio, Montana) where this project's own fact-checking process could not fully confirm when or whether the law took effect.

Data & sources

U.S. Election Assistance Commission
The federal survey every state files after each election, reporting how many mail ballots were sent, returned, and rejected. This is where every rejection-rate number on this page comes from — six elections, 2014–2024.
This project's own research
A hand-researched record of when each of the 51 states adopted its signature-cure law, checked in three separate rounds of fact-checking that caught and fixed 7 errors.
U.S. Census Bureau
County-level income, age, race, and the federal government's own urban/rural classification for every county, used in the rural-vs-urban comparison above.
This page
Every number shown here is a real, checked result — nothing is a placeholder or made up. The full technical writeup lives in this project's repository for anyone who wants to check the work.
